keyQuotes: As long as log remains, the mapping from probability to reward is unbounded, and any subsequent remedial measures are just dealing with the consequences.
Vanilla OPD is not a completely different design; it is the unbounded limit of PowerOPD when α=1.
The problem isn't that the post-processing is insufficient—it's log itself. What really needs to change is the mapping function from probability to reward.

mainPoints.explanation: Log diverges as probability approaches 0, leading to extreme rewards (negative tail near -50) and high-variance gradients, and this problem persists throughout training and is not eliminated by warmup.
mainPoints.point: The log-ratio reward in vanilla OPD is unbounded, which is the root cause of training instability.

mainPoints.explanation: These methods compress only after log has already magnified the values, which is too late; z-score can even flip the sign of the reward, causing incorrect learning direction and performing worse than no fix.
mainPoints.point: Post-hoc fixes such as clip, tanh, and z-score cannot fundamentally solve the problem.

mainPoints.explanation: PowerOPD satisfies boundedness ([-1,1]) and sign consistency (positive when teacher probability is higher, negative when student is higher, zero when equal), eliminating the unbounded issue at the mapping level.
mainPoints.point: PowerOPD replaces log with the Box-Cox power transformation, making the reward naturally bounded and sign-consistent.

mainPoints.explanation: α controls the degree to which reward magnitude is tied to absolute probability. Experiments show that larger α yields higher accuracy, shorter responses, and more stable training.
mainPoints.point: The parameter α acts as a 'probability region selector'; larger α focuses more on high-probability tokens, filtering low-probability noise.

mainPoints.explanation: The bottleneck of sampled-token OPD is not the sampling itself, but the reward shaping.
mainPoints.point: After replacing the unbounded log reward with a bounded power reward, sampled-token OPD becomes stronger, faster, and more resource-efficient than full-vocab OPD.

oneSentenceSummary: This paper diagnoses that the unbounded log-ratio reward in vanilla OPD causes training instability, and proposes PowerOPD, which replaces log with the Box-Cox power transformation, making the reward naturally bounded and sign-consistent. Experiments show it is more stable, stronger, and more resource-efficient.
originalTitle: 就从来没人质疑过 OPD 的 reward 设计吗？我们发现了 log 本身就是问题，也许就不该用！
summary: The article first points out that On-Policy Distillation (OPD) has become a standard component in post-training of large models, but mainstream sampled-token OPD (vanilla OPD) suffers from severe training pathologies: accuracy first drops then rises, response length oscillates, and final performance falls more than 8 points behind full-vocab OPD. By analyzing the reward distribution, the author identifies the root cause as the unbounded log-ratio reward (negative tail approaching -50), with extreme rewards concentrated in the early rollout stage and persisting throughout training. Comparing post-hoc fixes such as clip, tanh, and z-score, it is found that none can fundamentally solve the problem because log itself amplifies low-probability differences into extreme values. To address this, the author proposes PowerOPD: replacing log with the Box-Cox power transformation yields a family of bounded ([-1,1]) and sign-consistent rewards, and introduces a tunable parameter α as a "probability region selector" to filter low-probability noise. Experiments on multiple Qwen3 teacher-student settings and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that PowerOPD significantly outperforms vanilla OPD (average +4.47 Avg@8 / +4.06 Pass@8), surpasses all post-hoc methods, and even beats full-vocab OPD (up to +2.59 Avg@8 / +8.90 Pass@8), while saving 59.2% training time and 23.1% GPU memory. Gradient norm analysis reveals that PowerOPD gradients remain consistently in the 0.25-0.35 range, whereas vanilla OPD has an initial spike close to 1000 (a 3000x gap), demonstrating fundamental stability.
title: Has no one ever questioned OPD's reward design? We found that log itself is the problem—maybe it shouldn't be used!
